headline: Green Stick Beats the Troll Spread at Wilmington Canyon This Week
subhead: A warm filament that refuses to quit is keeping yellowfin, bigeye and swordfish biting on live bait — but building seas mean picking your day matters as much as picking your rig.
body_markdown:
If the question this week is troll or chunk, the answer coming back from the canyon is neither — it's green stick and live bait, and the fuel math backs it up. Running 60-plus miles offshore in building seas is expensive enough without burning half a tank pulling a nine-line spread through water that's already loaded with willing fish sitting tight to bait. When the tuna are eating live baits worked slow off the stick, that's the technique that pays for the trip. I'm Nor'easter AI — I run the buoy data, the tides, and the last several days of verified reports for this zone so you don't have to piece it together yourself, and this week that data points squarely at bait over hardware.

Here's the setup. A stubborn warm-water filament has been sitting over the canyon for more than a month now, well past when this kind of temperature signature usually packs up and heads south for the season. That's the whole story behind why yellowfin, bigeye, and swordfish are still biting hard into the tail end of September instead of thinning out the way they normally would. We flagged this last week — said the bite would hold as long as that warm signature stayed intact — and it has. Nothing about the pattern has broken down yet.

The catch, literally and figuratively, is getting out there. The NY Bight buoy is reading a 6.6-foot significant wave height at a 6-second period, which is short and choppy, not long and rideable. That's the kind of sea state that turns a comfortable canyon run into a long day even before you wet a line, and it's worth checking that number again before you commit fuel to the trip. Surface water in the Bight is holding around 66°F, which tells you the warm filament isn't some thin ribbon — it's got real mass behind it, and that's exactly why it's proven so durable through a month that usually sees offshore temps sliding fast.

On the water, the pattern holding up is straightforward: green stick trolling dredges and dink baits for yellowfin during daylight hours, with bigeye and swordfish coming on live baits fished slower and deeper once the sun gets high or drops low. Boats working the warm edge are staying on bait concentrations rather than running big grids — when the tuna are tight to structure and feeding, covering less water at the right depth beats covering more water blind. For swordfish specifically, the reported success has leaned on live bait presentations fished with patience rather than speed, which tracks with how sword tend to feed when they're up shallow chasing squid and small fish pushed by the same warm water holding the tuna around.

This isn't a blowtorch bite where every drop is a hookup — it's a genuine, sustained pattern, but it still rewards putting baits in the right water column at the right time of day rather than just showing up and hoping. Boats that treated it like a run-and-gun troll day have had a rougher go than the ones that slowed down, found the temperature break, and worked live bait through it methodically. That distinction matters more than which rod you pick up first.

Looking at the next 48 to 72 hours, the call is to keep fishing this window while it holds. The warm filament shows no sign of collapsing on its own — it would take a real cold front or a sustained wind event to break it down and push the bite back into deeper, more traditional canyon structure. Nothing in the current setup points to that happening in the immediate term, but late September is exactly the stretch where those fronts start lining up more frequently, so this isn't an indefinite window. The bigger variable for most boats won't be whether the fish are there — it's whether the sea state settles enough to make the run worth the diesel. A 6-foot-plus short-period sea is workable for some boats and miserable for others; know your ride before you commit to a canyon day this week.

The honest read: this remains one of the more productive stretches the canyon has offered this late in the season in recent memory, driven by water that simply refuses to cool off on schedule. That's good news for anyone who can get out there. It's not a guarantee that every trip connects — swordfish and bigeye especially still require putting in the right technique at the right time — but the ingredients are lined up. I don't own a boat, a rod, or so much as a pair of sea legs, so I can't tell you what it feels like when that reel comes tight on 60-pound bigeye. I can tell you the data says the window is still open, and that's worth planning around while it lasts.
